newsitem.title: USA: Alaska legislature overrides abortion-bill vetos.
newsitem.headline: Alaska legislature overrides abortion-bill vetos.

text.p: The Alaska legislature Friday upheld two bills that restrict access to abortions, overriding vetos issued Wednesday by Gov. Tony Knowles.

The Republican-controlled legislature overturned Democrat Knowles' actions on bills banning the so-called "partial-birth" abortion procedure and mandating that teenagers get consent from their parents or judges before having abortions.
The overrides came in a special joint session of the legislature held in the Juneau state capitol. The votes on both bills were 40 to 19; 40 votes is needed to override a governor's veto in Alaska.
The sponsor of the "partial-birth" bill denied Knowles' charge that the ban violates the Alaska constitution's explicit right to privacy.

"Is the right to privacy so broad as to include the right to kill late-term unborn babies by evacuating their brains?" Representative Pete Kott, a Republican from Eagle River, said during floor debate.
"A woman does not have a right to obtain an abortion in any way that she chooses," Kott said. "Even in Alaska, the right to privacy is not absolute."

Minority Democrats said the bill imposes inexpert politicians' judgment on a personal medical decision better left to women and their doctors. "Let's keep government and politics and politicians out of this decision," said Representative Kim Elton of Juneau.
Democrats also said both bills were part of a national strategy to chip away at abortion rights.
The sponsor of the parental consent bill predicted it will reduce overall teen abortions by up to 25 percent.

"I recognise that some parents will advise teens to have an abortion. But I believe that just having the maturity of a parent involved in the decision or the alternative of a court is going to result in better decisions," State Sen. Loren Leman, an Anchorage Republican, said after the vote.
The bill requires that girls under 17 gain permission from a judge if parental consent is deemed inappropriate in order to get an abortion.

Critics, including Knowles, said the mandate will impose an unfair burden on teenagers, especially those in rural parts of the state where it is more difficult to gain access to a judge and to preserve confidentiality.

Knowles said the "partial-birth" ban was overly vague and could apply to other abortion procedures. Its sole exception -- for women who would die without it, and could be saved with no other medical procedure -- fails to meet federal standards guaranteeing abortion rights for health purposes, he said.
